name: Greed (avaritia) as capital vice
plainSummary: In this list, greed denotes a disordered love of possessing—holding or seeking wealth in a way that subordinates justice, charity, or the common good.
description: Derived principle: avaritia (greed or covetousness) is the capital vice of excessive attachment to material goods, including insatiable acquisition and hoarding, classically contrasted with liberality and justice.
foundationStrengthRationale: Widely echoed in religious and secular critiques of exploitation; boundaries between prudent provision and disordered attachment remain debated.

pros.claim: Illuminates structural harms when acquisition eclipses duty to others.
pros.evidence: Traditions link greed to fraud, usury (in historical sense), neglect of the poor, and environmental overreach.

cons.claim: Risk of moralizing wealth without distinguishing legitimate enterprise, saving, and innovation.
cons.evidence: Market societies debate when profit-seeking is productive versus exploitative; blanket talk of greed can oversimplify.
